hook.line: Vale needs a new space for the café, and all she can do is describe it: a proper kitchen, a rent she can pay. She can't point at it yet, and Spanish has a way of saying so.
hook.es: Buscamos un lugar que tenga cocina.
hook.en: We're looking for a place that has a kitchen.

examples.en: I'm looking for an apartment that has two bedrooms.

examples.es: Busco el apartamento que tiene dos cuartos.
examples.en: I'm looking for the apartment that has two bedrooms.

rule:
Ask one question: do I know this thing exists?

Yes, I can point at it: the ordinary ending.
*Tengo un amigo que sabe de leyes.* He exists.
*Busco el apartamento que tiene balcón.* I know which one.

No, I'm only describing what I want, or there may be none: the wish ending, the same one you know from *quiero que*.
*Busco un apartamento que tenga balcón.* Any one that fits.
*No conozco a nadie que sepa.* Nobody, so no real person to point at.

English uses the same verb both times (that has, who knows). Spanish changes the ending: *tiene* becomes *tenga*, *sabe* becomes *sepa*, *es* becomes *sea*.

The verb after *que* tells your listener whether the thing is real or only wished for.
smallPrint: Teachers call this a relative clause with an unspecified or non-existent antecedent: the subjunctive goes in the clause that describes it.

yourTurn.prompt: Pick *tiene* or *tenga* and type the whole sentence: *Busco una casa que ___ jardín.* (I'm looking for a house that has a garden, any one, I don't know if one exists.)
yourTurn.answer: Busco una casa que tenga jardín.
yourTurn.why: You don't know that such a house exists, so the verb takes the wish ending: *tenga*.

yourTurn.prompt: Pick *sabe* or *sepa* and type the whole sentence: *Tengo un amigo que ___ de leyes.* (I have a friend who knows about law.)
yourTurn.answer: Tengo un amigo que sabe de leyes.
yourTurn.why: You have this friend, so he is real and the verb keeps the ordinary ending: *sabe*.

yourTurn.prompt: Say: We're looking for a kitchen that is big.
yourTurn.answer: Buscamos una cocina que sea grande.
accept: Estamos buscando una cocina que sea grande.
yourTurn.why: You're describing what you want, not a kitchen you've seen, so *que sea*.

yourTurn.prompt: Say: Do you know anyone who speaks English? (to a friend)
yourTurn.why: You're asking whether such a person exists, so *hable*, not *habla*.

yourTurn.prompt: Say: I need a room that has a window.
yourTurn.answer: Necesito un cuarto que tenga ventana.
yourTurn.why: Any room with a window will do, so *tenga*.

yourTurn.prompt: Make it negative, there is nobody: *Conozco a alguien que sabe de leyes.*
yourTurn.answer: No conozco a nadie que sepa de leyes.
yourTurn.why: With *nadie* there is nobody to point at, so the verb takes *sepa*.

yourTurn.prompt: Now you have a specific apartment in mind: *Busco un apartamento que tenga balcón.* Say: I'm looking for the apartment that has a balcony.
yourTurn.answer: Busco el apartamento que tiene balcón.
yourTurn.why: You know which apartment, so *el apartamento* and the ordinary *tiene*.

pitfalls.wrong: Busco un apartamento que tiene dos cuartos.
pitfalls.right: Busco un apartamento que tenga dos cuartos.
pitfalls.why: Almost. You haven't found it yet, so the verb after *que* takes the wish ending: *tenga*.

pitfalls.wrong: No conozco a nadie que sabe de leyes.
pitfalls.right: No conozco a nadie que sepa de leyes.
pitfalls.why: Almost. *Nadie* means there is nobody real to point at, so *sepa*.

pitfalls.wrong: Tengo un amigo que sepa de leyes.
pitfalls.right: Tengo un amigo que sabe de leyes.
pitfalls.why: Almost. You do have this friend, so he is real and the verb stays ordinary: *sabe*.

pitfalls.wrong: Busco el apartamento que tenga balcón.
pitfalls.right: Busco el apartamento que tiene balcón.
pitfalls.why: Almost. *El apartamento* is one you already know about, so the verb is ordinary: *tiene*.

personal: Say what you'd look for in a new place to live, real or not: start with *Busco un lugar que…* and finish with something that matters to you, like *tenga* a kitchen or *sea* quiet.
